::: {.callout-note}
**This chapter is about combining data that arrives in more than one piece.**

**Assumed knowledge:** Sessions 2 and 3 — loading a DataFrame, filtering, and cleaning
text columns. The text-cleaning part matters here: **you cannot join on a key you have
not cleaned.**

**The one idea to take away:** every join can silently lose rows or silently multiply
them. **Print the row count before and after. Every time.**
:::

## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s04-outcomes}

By the end of this chapter you can:

1. Describe the five approaches to data integration and pick one for a situation.
2. Stack tables with `concat` and link tables with `merge`.
3. Use all four join types and predict how many rows each returns.
4. Detect a join that lost rows and a join that multiplied them.
5. Fix the three things that break a join: mismatched keys, different names for the
   same thing, and duplicate keys.

# Part A — Five ways to integrate {#sec-s04-a}

## 1. Why data is never in one place {#sec-s04-topic-1}

**Data integration is combining data from several sources into one view you can
analyse.**

It exists because organisations do not store data for the convenience of analysts. Sales
sit in the sales system, support tickets in the helpdesk, web visits in the analytics
tool. Each was built for its own job. **The question "do customers who contact support
buy less?" touches all three, and no single system can answer it.**

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the wedding guest list"}
One partner keeps family names in a notebook; the other keeps friends in a spreadsheet.
Neither list is wrong. But you cannot count chairs, order food or print place cards
until they are one list.

**The painful part is not the copying — it is that "R. Sharma" and "Raj Sharma" might be
the same person, or might be two people.** That question is the whole of data
integration.
:::

## 2. The five approaches {#sec-s04-topic-2}

**There are five ways to combine sources. They differ in one thing: how much data you
copy, and who does the translating.**

| Approach | What happens | Data is copied? | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Physical** (data warehouse) | copy everything into one central database on a schedule | **yes** | fast queries; one place to look | data is as old as the last copy; expensive |
| **Virtual** (federation) | leave data where it is; a layer queries each source live when asked | **no** | always current; nothing to store | slow; breaks when any source is down |
| **Application-based** | each application translates and pushes its own data to the others | partly | no central system needed | every app must know about every other; *n* apps means many links |
| **Middleware** | one translation layer sits between sources and converts formats | partly | apps stay simple; one place to fix | the middleware becomes a single point of failure |
| **Manual** | a person exports CSVs and combines them by hand | yes | needs nothing; works today | slow, unrepeatable, **and error-prone** |

### How to choose

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Q1{"Does the answer have to be<br/>up to the second?"}
    Q1 -- yes --> V["<b>Virtual</b><br/>query the sources live"]
    Q1 -- no --> Q2{"Will the same question<br/>be asked repeatedly?"}
    Q2 -- no --> M["<b>Manual</b><br/>a one-off export is fine"]
    Q2 -- yes --> Q3{"Many systems that must<br/>talk to each other?"}
    Q3 -- yes --> MW["<b>Middleware</b><br/>one translation layer"]
    Q3 -- no --> P["<b>Physical</b><br/>copy into a warehouse"]
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Manual integration is where most reporting errors come from"}
Copying and pasting between spreadsheets leaves no record of what was done, cannot be
repeated identically, and fails silently when a column shifts by one. **If a manual
integration is going to happen more than twice, write the code instead.**
:::

### ❓ Check yourself

**Q1.** A dashboard must show live warehouse stock, and stock changes every few seconds.
Which approach?

- (a) Physical integration into a nightly warehouse.
- (b) **Virtual integration, querying the stock system directly.**
- (c) Manual integration.

**Q2.** Twelve internal systems each need data from the other eleven, and every team is
writing its own converter. Which approach fixes this?

- (a) Manual integration.
- (b) Virtual integration.
- (c) **Middleware — one translation layer instead of many pairwise converters.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
**A1 — (b).** A nightly copy would show yesterday's stock, which for this question is
worse than useless. Virtual integration trades speed for freshness, and freshness is
what this dashboard is for.

**A2 — (c).** With 12 systems talking directly, you can end up maintaining dozens of
converters. Middleware means each system talks to one thing.
:::

# Part B — Doing it in pandas {#sec-s04-b}

## 3. Stacking versus linking {#sec-s04-topic-3}

**There are two different operations, and mixing them up is the most common beginner
error.**

| Operation | Question it answers | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Stacking** | "here are more rows of the same thing" | `pd.concat` |
| **Linking** | "here is extra information about the same things" | `pd.merge` |

Two months of sales → **stack**. Customers and their orders → **link**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    subgraph S["concat — stacking"]
        A1["Jan sales<br/>100 rows"] --> C1["200 rows<br/>same columns"]
        A2["Feb sales<br/>100 rows"] --> C1
    end
    subgraph M["merge — linking"]
        B1["customers<br/>name, city"] --> C2["one row per match<br/>more columns"]
        B2["orders<br/>amount, date"] --> C2
    end
```

### Demo 1 — stacking with concat

```{python}
import pandas as pd

jan = pd.DataFrame({"date": ["2024-01-05", "2024-01-19"], "amount": [250, 90]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"date": ["2024-02-02", "2024-02-27"], "amount": [410, 130]})

stacked = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True)
print(stacked)
print(f"\n{len(jan)} + {len(feb)} = {len(stacked)} rows. Columns unchanged: {list(stacked.columns)}")
```

`ignore_index=True` renumbers the rows. Without it you get row labels 0, 1, 0, 1 — two
rows labelled 0, which causes confusing errors later.

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ concat lines columns up by *name*"}
If one month's file calls the column `amount` and the other calls it `Amount`, `concat`
does not complain. It creates **both** columns and fills each with blanks where the other
was used. **Check `.columns` on both tables before stacking.**
:::

```{python}
mismatched = pd.DataFrame({"date": ["2024-03-01"], "Amount": [500]})   # capital A
oops = pd.concat([jan, mismatched], ignore_index=True)
print(oops)
print("\nTwo amount columns, both half empty — and no error was raised.")
```

## 4. Linking tables with merge {#sec-s04-topic-4}

**`merge` joins two tables using a shared column called the key.** The key is usually an
ID.

### Demo 2 — a first merge

```{python}
import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "user_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "name":    ["Alice", "Bob", "Chan", "Devi"],
    "city":    ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Mumbai", "Pune"],
})

purchases = pd.DataFrame({
    "purchase_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "user_id":     [1, 1, 3, 5],       # Alice bought twice; user 5 is not in customers
    "amount":      [250.0, 120.0, 75.5, 300.0],
})

print("customers:"); print(customers)
print("\npurchases:"); print(purchases)

joined = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="inner")
print("\nInner join:"); print(joined)
print(f"\ncustomers {len(customers)} rows + purchases {len(purchases)} rows → {len(joined)} rows")
```

Read that row count carefully. **Four and four made three.** Bob and Devi vanished
(no purchases), user 5 vanished (not a known customer), and Alice appears twice (two
purchases). This is normal, and it is why you check.

## 5. The four join types {#sec-s04-topic-5}

**The join type answers one question: which rows do you keep when there is no match?**

| Type | Keeps | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `inner` | only rows matching in **both** | you need complete records |
| `left` | **all** left rows; blanks where no match | the left table is your population |
| `right` | **all** right rows | rare — usually a `left` with the tables swapped |
| `outer` | **everything** from both | you are looking for what does not match |

### Demo 3 — all four, on the same two tables

```{python}
for how in ["inner", "left", "right", "outer"]:
    result = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how=how)
    names = result["name"].fillna("(unknown)").tolist()
    print(f"{how:>6}: {len(result)} rows — {names}")
```

Now read what each one is *for*:

```{python}
print("LEFT — every customer, whether or not they bought anything:")
left = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left")
print(left[["name", "city", "amount"]])

print("\nWho has never bought anything? The rows where amount is blank:")
print(left[left["amount"].isna()]["name"].tolist())

print("\nOUTER — everything, including the purchase by an unknown user 5:")
outer = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="outer")
print(outer[outer["name"].isna()][["user_id", "purchase_id", "amount"]])
```

**The `left` join answered a business question the `inner` join could not**: which
customers have never purchased. An inner join deletes exactly those people.

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the class register"}
`inner` — students who are on the register **and** sat the exam.
`left` — the whole register; those who missed the exam show a blank mark.
`outer` — the register plus any exam papers from people who are not on it.

**The blanks are not a nuisance. They are usually the finding.**
:::

## 6. Aggregate, then join {#sec-s04-topic-6}

**When one side has many rows per key, joining directly multiplies rows. Usually you
want a summary instead.**

### Demo 4 — one row per customer

```{python}
# Wrong for most purposes: Alice appears twice, so any count of customers is now wrong.
naive = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left")
print(f"Naive join: {len(naive)} rows for {len(customers)} customers")

# Right: summarise the many side first, then join one-to-one.
per_customer = purchases.groupby("user_id").agg(
    n_purchases=("purchase_id", "count"),
    total_spent=("amount", "sum"),
).reset_index()

summary = pd.merge(customers, per_customer, on="user_id", how="left")
summary["n_purchases"] = summary["n_purchases"].fillna(0).astype(int)
summary["total_spent"] = summary["total_spent"].fillna(0)

print(f"\nAggregate-then-join: {len(summary)} rows for {len(customers)} customers")
print(summary)
```

**One row per customer, every customer present, spending totalled.** This
aggregate-then-join pattern is the one you will use most often in real work.

# Part C — What goes wrong {#sec-s04-c}

## 7. The three failures {#sec-s04-topic-7}

### Failure 1 — the key does not match

**The most common cause of "the join returned nothing".** The keys look identical to a
human and differ to a computer.

```{python}
left_tbl  = pd.DataFrame({"email": ["ASHA@mail.com", "brij@mail.com "], "plan": ["gold", "silver"]})
right_tbl = pd.DataFrame({"email": ["asha@mail.com", "brij@mail.com"],  "spend": [900, 400]})

print("Joining as-is:")
print(pd.merge(left_tbl, right_tbl, on="email", how="inner"))
print("→ 0 rows. One key has capitals, the other has a trailing space.\n")

for t in (left_tbl, right_tbl):
    t["email"] = t["email"].str.strip().str.lower()

print("After cleaning the key:")
print(pd.merge(left_tbl, right_tbl, on="email", how="inner"))
```

**Clean the key before you join.** Trim spaces, fix the case, standardise the format.
This is why Session 3 comes before this chapter.

### Failure 2 — the same thing, different column names

```{python}
orders = pd.DataFrame({"cust_ref": [1, 2], "total": [500, 250]})   # different key name

merged = pd.merge(customers, orders, left_on="user_id", right_on="cust_ref", how="inner")
print(merged[["user_id", "name", "cust_ref", "total"]])
print("\n`left_on` and `right_on` join columns that mean the same thing but are named differently.")
```

### Failure 3 — duplicate keys multiply rows

**This is the dangerous one, because nothing fails.** The code runs, the model trains,
the numbers look plausible, and they are wrong.

```{python}
# A dirty reference table: 'Mumbai' listed twice by mistake.
regions = pd.DataFrame({
    "city":   ["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Mumbai"],
    "region": ["West", "North", "West", "West"],
})

blown_up = pd.merge(customers, regions, on="city", how="left")
print(f"customers: {len(customers)} rows  →  after joining regions: {len(blown_up)} rows")
print(blown_up[["user_id", "name", "city", "region"]])
print("\nAlice and Chan each appear twice. Every total computed from this table is now")
print("double-counted for Mumbai — and nothing raised an error.")

# The fix: make sure the lookup table has one row per key before joining.
regions_clean = regions.drop_duplicates(subset="city")
fixed = pd.merge(customers, regions_clean, on="city", how="left")
print(f"\nAfter de-duplicating the lookup table: {len(fixed)} rows")
```

## 8. The check that catches all three {#sec-s04-topic-8}

**One helper function, used after every join, catches every failure in this chapter.**

```{python}
def check_join(left, right, result, name="join"):
    """Report what a join did to the row count, and whether keys went unmatched."""
    print(f"{name}: left {len(left)} × right {len(right)} → result {len(result)}")
    if len(result) > len(left):
        print(f"  ⚠ GREW by {len(result)-len(left)} rows — the right table has duplicate keys")
    elif len(result) < len(left):
        print(f"  ⚠ SHRANK by {len(left)-len(result)} rows — some left keys had no match")
    else:
        print("  ✓ one row in, one row out")
    blanks = result.isna().sum()
    if blanks.any():
        print(f"  unmatched values appear as blanks in: {blanks[blanks>0].to_dict()}")

check_join(customers, regions, blown_up, "customers + dirty regions")
print()
check_join(customers, regions_clean, fixed, "customers + clean regions")
print()
check_join(customers, purchases, pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id"), "customers + purchases (inner)")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ A join that changes the row count is a claim, not an accident"}
A shrinking join says *"these records had no match"*. A growing join says *"one of these
keys is not unique"*. Both may be fine — but **you should be able to say which, and
why**, before you use the result.
:::

### ❓ Check yourself

**Q3.** You have 1,000 customers and join a `city → region` lookup. You get 1,043 rows.
What happened?

- (a) 43 customers were added.
- (b) **The lookup table has duplicate city entries, so some customers matched twice.**
- (c) The join type was wrong.

**Q4.** You want every product listed in a sales report, including those that sold
nothing this month. Which join?

- (a) `inner`, from sales to products.
- (b) **`left`, from products to sales.**
- (c) `right`, from products to sales.

**Q5.** A merge on `email` returns 0 rows even though both tables clearly contain the
same people. Most likely cause?

- (a) Pandas is broken.
- (b) **The keys differ in case or whitespace.**
- (c) The tables are too large.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"}
**A3 — (b).** Demo in Failure 3. Every total computed afterwards is inflated for the
duplicated cities.

**A4 — (b).** Start from the table whose rows you want to keep all of. Products with no
sales come through with blank sales figures — which is exactly the answer you wanted.

**A5 — (b).** Failure 1. `"ASHA@mail.com"` and `"asha@mail.com"` are different strings.
:::

# 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s04-tasks}

::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"}
**Task 1 — Predict, then check.** Before running anything, write down how many rows each
of the four join types will return for `customers` and `purchases`. Then run Demo 3.
**Report which you got wrong and why.**

**Task 2 — Find the silent customers.** Using a left join, list every customer who has
never made a purchase.

**Task 3 — Break it, then fix it.** Add a second `"Delhi"` row to the `regions` table.
Join, and use `check_join` to detect the damage. Then fix it.

**Task 4 — Aggregate then join.** Produce a table with one row per **city** showing the
number of customers and the total amount spent by customers in that city.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
```{python}
import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({"user_id": [1,2,3,4], "name": ["Alice","Bob","Chan","Devi"],
                          "city": ["Mumbai","Delhi","Mumbai","Pune"]})
purchases = pd.DataFrame({"purchase_id": [101,102,103,104], "user_id": [1,1,3,5],
                          "amount": [250.0,120.0,75.5,300.0]})

# Task 1 — inner 3, left 5, right 4, outer 6
for how in ["inner","left","right","outer"]:
    print(f"Task 1 — {how:>6}: {len(pd.merge(customers, purchases, on='user_id', how=how))} rows")

# Task 2
left = pd.merge(customers, purchases, on="user_id", how="left")
print("\nTask 2 — never purchased:", left[left["amount"].isna()]["name"].tolist())

# Task 4 — aggregate the many side, then join, then group by city
per_cust = purchases.groupby("user_id")["amount"].sum().reset_index(name="spent")
by_city = (pd.merge(customers, per_cust, on="user_id", how="left")
             .assign(spent=lambda d: d["spent"].fillna(0))
             .groupby("city")
             .agg(customers=("user_id","count"), total_spent=("spent","sum")))
print("\nTask 4:"); print(by_city)
```
::::

::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"}
- [ ] I can name all five integration approaches and choose between them
- [ ] I know when to `concat` and when to `merge`
- [ ] I can predict the row count of an inner, left, right and outer join
- [ ] I clean the key column before joining on it
- [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** check the row count after every join. A join that
      quietly doubles rows produces totals that are wrong and never raises an error.
:::
